clue.text: Business with many branches to manage?

definitions.text: Business with many branches to manage?

blocks.note: surface reading: a chain company with outlets in many towns
setter's reading: the branches are on trees, and the business is looking after woodland

explanation.walkthrough: 'Branches' suggests a bank or retail chain; the question mark warns that the branches are literal ones growing on trees.
explanation.definitionFit: The trade of planting, tending and harvesting woodland is a business whose stock is trees, each with many limbs.

clue.text: In the end, if you stress, that’s trouble

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only the closing letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the final letters of these four words

explanation.surface: Advice that getting stressed only causes more trouble in the long run.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of that's is its last letter, so it supplies the final S; the rest of the word works as the link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe needless commotion and bother, as in 'don't go to any trouble' or 'don't make a fuss'.

clue.text: Strengthening check for building material

blocks.note: to rein in is to check or restrain
taken as written
cement is a binding material used in construction

explanation.surface: A builder's inspection to see which materials will make a structure stronger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Check' reads as an inspection noun, but it is a verb meaning restrain, as one holds a horse back with the reins.
explanation.definitionFit: Making something stronger or supporting it is the act of reinforcing, so the noun forms are direct synonyms.

clue.text: Place to buy rump steak and, er, nuts

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters go wild and end up in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A shopping list naming where to buy steak and, after a hesitation, some nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' looks like an item on the list beside the steak, but it is the signal; the hesitant 'er' contributes its two letters to the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A large self-service grocery store is a typical shop where people purchase food and household goods.

clue.text: Name of dance almost taking place

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the word loses its final letter
to take something in is to hold it, so one piece receives another inside it

blocks.note: a reel is a lively Scottish dance, here missing its last letter
to place something is to put it

explanation.surface: Asking what a dance that is currently happening is called.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Name of dance' tempts you to look for a dance name, but 'Name' alone is the definition. REE holds PUT to give RE(PUT)E.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's good name is their standing or reputation, which is what repute means as a noun.

clue.text: Stimulate short burst of activity briefly

indicators.note: briefly means in a curtailed way, so the word drops its final letter

blocks.note: a spurt is a short burst of effort, trimmed of its last letter

explanation.surface: Encouraging someone with a quick, intense bout of effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' belongs to the description of a spurt, not to the cutting signal; it is 'briefly' that removes the T.
explanation.definitionFit: To spur someone on is to urge or incite them, from the rider's spur that prods a horse forward.

clue.text: Official statements president finally makes about rental agreements

indicators.note: finally points to what comes at the very end, so just the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: PRES is a standard abbreviation for president
the last letter of this word
RE means about or concerning
a lease is a contract for renting property

explanation.surface: A president at last issuing statements on housing contracts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'President finally' looks like it wants the last letter of president, but 'finally' applies to 'makes'; president is shortened to PRES.
explanation.definitionFit: Announcements issued to journalists by an organisation are formal statements given out for publication.

clue.text: Objected to being introduced without a leader

indicators.note: a leader is the one at the front, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: presented means introduced, with the opening P dropped

explanation.surface: Someone annoyed at being brought forward without anyone in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: PRESENTED, as a host presents a guest, loses its first letter to leave RESENTED.
explanation.definitionFit: To resent something is to feel bitter or indignant about it, taking exception much as one who protests does.

clue.text: Cut back on spending, maybe primarily in spring

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is kept
one piece placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: to skip is to spring or hop lightly
the first letter of this word

explanation.surface: A household deciding to economise, perhaps during the spring season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' reads as the season but is the verb meaning leap, giving SKIP, which holds M to make SKI(M)P.
explanation.definitionFit: To skimp is to be stingy or economise, using less money or material than is really needed.

clue.text: Have gangs succeeded?

blocks.note: a posse is a band of people, especially one pursuing someone
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in family trees

explanation.surface: Asking whether criminal gangs have pulled off their plans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have' reads as an auxiliary verb starting a question, but it is the definition; S for succeeded is a dictionary abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To possess something is to own or hold it, a direct synonym for having it.

clue.text: Great political orator to provide letters in order for file?

blocks.note: to spell a word is to give its letters in sequence
a binder is a folder for holding filed papers

explanation.surface: A speaker who lays out letters neatly for filing, as if an orator did office work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' and 'file' paint an office scene; the letters are the alphabet ones you spell, and the file needs something to hold it.
explanation.definitionFit: A speaker who holds an audience entranced is said to cast a spell on them, especially a captivating public speaker.

clue.text: Gold medal winner Adam?

blocks.note: first meaning: whoever comes first in a contest
second meaning: in Genesis, the earliest human created

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an athlete called Adam, such as swimmer Adam Peaty; the two parts are separate meanings of one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A champion is the individual placed at the top, while the biblical Adam was the original man God created.

clue.text: Badly beat, slam and reprimand

indicators.note: something done badly is done wrongly, so the letters come out in the wrong order

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A thrashing followed by harsh criticism, someone soundly beaten then told off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly beat' reads as a violent phrase, but 'Badly' is the signal working on both following words.
explanation.definitionFit: To lambaste is to criticise someone harshly, a strong version of telling them off severely.

clue.text: A secondary route out of the country

blocks.note: taken as written
British roads are classed A (main) and B (secondary), so a minor road is a B followed by the word for a route

explanation.surface: A back road being used as an escape route across the border.
explanation.walkthrough: In the UK, roads are classed as A roads (main) and B roads (secondary), so a secondary route is a B ROAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Being abroad means being in a foreign land, away from one's home nation.

clue.text: Wool coat to take to the cleaners?

blocks.note: first meaning: the woolly covering of a sheep
second meaning: to swindle someone out of their money

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests carrying a woollen coat to the dry cleaner; 'take to the cleaners' is an idiom for cheating someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheep's shorn woolly hide is its natural covering, and overcharging or swindling a victim is to rob them blind.

clue.text: Series of online messages is extremely tough to browse through

indicators.note: extremes are the two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of this word
to read is to look through a text

explanation.surface: Complaining that a long online discussion is very hard to get through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely tough' reads as 'very hard', but 'extremely' means the extreme letters of 'tough'.
explanation.definitionFit: On forums and email, a chain of replies on one topic is called a thread, like a strand linking posts.

clue.text: Start chatting in work downtime with new techie

indicators.note: something new has been remade, so these letters take a fresh form

blocks.note: a break is a rest period at work
taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Getting a conversation going during a work break with the newly hired IT person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New techie' reads as a recent hire, but 'new' signals that TECHIE is rearranged into THE ICE.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means easing initial awkwardness to get a conversation going between strangers.

clue.text: Venture to take on old politician

indicators.note: to take something on is to take it aboard, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: to venture is to try or attempt
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Daring to challenge a veteran politician.
explanation.walkthrough: TRY holds O to give T(O)RY; a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party, so an example of a politician.

clue.text: Cover of outbuilding mostly retains warmth

indicators.note: mostly means not entirely, so the word loses its final letter
to retain is to keep hold of, so one piece holds another inside it

blocks.note: a shed is an outbuilding, cut short here
heat is warmth

explanation.surface: The roof of a shed keeps the heat in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' reads as a noun, the roof of the shed, but it is a verb; SHE holds HEAT to make S(HEAT)HE.
explanation.definitionFit: To sheathe is to encase or wrap something in a protective casing, as a sword goes into its scabbard.

clue.text: ’70s music record with keyboards in the middle

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its centre, so only the central letter is kept

blocks.note: a disc is a gramophone record
the central letter of this nine-letter word

explanation.surface: A 1970s record with synthesiser parts in its central section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keyboards' suggests instruments on the record, but its job is to give its middle letter, the fifth of nine.
explanation.definitionFit: Disco was the dance style that dominated popular music in the late 1970s, so it is a genre of that decade.

clue.text: Some treat-size food

indicators.note: some means a part of, so the letters come from a portion of the words

blocks.note: letters running across the hyphen

explanation.surface: Snacks sold in small portions as a treat.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from inside 'treat' into 'size', bridging the hyphen.
explanation.definitionFit: Eats is an informal plural noun for things to eat, especially snacks or a meal.

clue.text: Suspect is ready to admit anything at first, probably

indicators.note: at first points to the beginning, so only the opening letter is kept
something suspect is dubious and not as it seems, so the letters are rearranged
admitting lets something in, so an extra letter joins the mix before shuffling

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
the first letter of this word

explanation.surface: A police suspect who is likely ready to confess to anything at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' reads as a noun, the person under arrest, but is an adjective signalling the rearrangement; 'admit' reads as confess but means let in.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a mild way of conceding something is likely, used much like 'I suppose' or 'presumably'.
